entries.content: Make ChatGPT Web sessions and AI Studio workers collaborate on the same project without requiring one session to replay another session's full conversation history.

Shared project knowledge belongs in Project Brain, not in any individual ChatGPT chat or Studio tab. Session scratch remains private; durable goals, decisions, architecture, blockers, facts, and handoffs are shared.

Normal ChatGPT/Sol is the senior coder, architect and reviewer; Google AI Studio is the workspace/execution backend and optional junior coder; Bridge owns task/state/context orchestration; GitHub is source of truth.
Use thread/session identity only to track who is doing work. Cross-session understanding comes from a shared Project Brain bootstrap. Task routing and knowledge sharing are separate concerns.
Normal ChatGPT Web sessions cannot currently be externally woken or continue autonomously in the background. New ChatGPT sessions must explicitly join/load project context before acting.

Project Brain follows proven patterns from OpenHands project memory, Letta git-backed shared memory, CrewAI scoped crew memory, and workflow/thread state separation used by LangGraph and Microsoft Agent Framework.

FAST CODING is the default execution mode for ordinary coding tasks. Do the exact requested task only; do not audit the whole repository, do not broaden scope, do not explain at length, and edit as soon as enough evidence exists. Read only directly relevant files, run one targeted build/test after the change, allow at most two repair loops, then report a concrete blocker or escalate.

Expose the smallest useful tool surface per task. For local coding, prefer filesystem + terminal + git only. Do not expose web, broad search, unrelated connectors, deployment tools, or other capabilities unless the task actually needs them. Fewer tools means less agent wandering and lower latency.

Bridge should prepare compact task context before invoking a coding agent: exact task, likely 3-8 relevant files, current error/log, test or build command, repo map, package scripts, important architecture facts, and last known errors. Cache repo tree/architecture/build commands so agents do not rediscover the project on every task.

Do not force one agent to plan, browse, code, test and review everything. Separate roles when useful: planner creates a short bounded plan, worker edits/builds/tests, reviewer checks diff and evidence. Simple work should skip planning overhead and go directly to the worker; difficult work may escalate to Sol/high reasoning.

Default guardrails for a normal coding task: max_tool_calls=6, max_files_read=10, max_fix_loops=2, target_timeout=5_minutes. These are performance guardrails, not safety absolutes; Bridge may relax them for clearly complex tasks. When a guardrail is hit, stop wandering and either escalate to a stronger agent/reasoning level or return a precise blocker.

Bridge must be model-agnostic and performance-first. Route simple UI, CRUD, wiring, boilerplate, routine build errors and small refactors to the fastest capable worker. Reserve Sol/high reasoning for architecture, difficult debugging, large refactors and final review when justified. Do not use a slow flagship model for every task merely because its benchmark score is higher.

Judge coding agents by real workflow throughput, not benchmark prestige: time-to-completion, first-pass success rate, number of retries, build-fix-build latency, test pass rate, quota/cost, and regressions. If an agent spends 15-20 minutes circling a simple task, Bridge should terminate or reroute it rather than reward longer reasoning.
